content: Obstructive sleep apnoea occurs due to the temporary closure of the upper airway during sleep. This condition can progress into hypopnoea, where the airway narrows but still allows some airflow. The underlying cause is an imbalance between the forces compressing the airway and those maintaining its openness. Obesity is the most common factor associated with obstructive sleep apnoea, as fatty tissue accumulates around the airway, contributing to its collapse. Exercise has been proposed as a method to promote weight loss, which is believed to alleviate symptoms of obstructive sleep apnoea. Other weight loss strategies are also thought to improve the condition. Additionally, sleep hygiene practices may influence the structure of sleep and the regulation of the upper airway, potentially enhancing its stability during sleep. The purpose of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness of weight loss, sleep hygiene, and exercise in managing obstructive sleep apnoea. To achieve this, databases such as the Cochrane Airways Group Specialised Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, and CINAHL, as well as reference lists from review articles, were searched. The most recent search was conducted in April 2009. The inclusion criteria for this review required randomised, singleor double-blind, placebo-controlled studies with either a parallel group or crossover design that investigated any of these interventions. However, no completed trials meeting these criteria were identified. An updated search revealed one study available only in abstract form, and the results of another ongoing study are still awaited. The authors concluded that there is a significant need for randomised controlled trials to evaluate these commonly used treatments for obstructive sleep apnoea. Future studies should aim to identify specific subgroups of patients who benefit most from each intervention and should employ clear and standardised outcome measures.
